new_statements.quote: The nucleus of each stress group is a syllable marked by increased intensity which also causes slight rising of pitch and a tendency towards length. [...] The occurrence of stress in any word is unpredictable but it defines a syllable on which it falls as being one of the three last syllables of the stress group. Stress on an open syllable of the base in manifested by length, and this length remains on the syllable as the stress moves. Affixation of the base causes the stress to remain in the same position relative to the last syllable. If this is an open syllable it will also be lengthened. [...] Length is the minimal difference between many words [...] sa.lay 'egg' salay 'a tree used for making paddles'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (intensity + pitch rise, realised as vowel length on open syllables) is lexically contrastive and not predictable, but confined to a three-syllable window at the right edge of the stress group (word plus clitics); under suffixation stress shifts rightward so as to keep its distance from the final syllable, while the base's stressed open vowel keeps its length; monosyllabic enclitic pronouns do not affect stress placement. The Webonary dictionary accordingly marks stress in the pronunciation field of each headword.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is said to be predictable from primary stress: in reduplicated forms it falls on the syllable that is stressed in the base; otherwise on the second syllable following, or the third syllable preceding, the primary stress; it is deleted if that third-preceding syllable is itself preceded by a stressed syllable; apparent second-preceding cases arise from vowel syncope. It has the same correlates as primary stress (incl. length on open syllables) but weaker, especially in pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: Author flags that data are insufficient to predict stress change under change of grammatical class, and that stress movement/predictability needs further study (Sec. 5); in bases with penultimate stress the only stop allowed in the coda of the penult is glottal stop; gemination from vowel syncope can shift stress (alalaki ~ allaki 'bigger'); suprasegmentals are not written in the practical orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the 'stress group' (base plus affixes and monosyllabic clitics; polysyllabic pronouns/particle strings form their own stress group), i.e. essentially the phonological word in connected speech; explicitly a 'preliminary' tagmemic-hierarchy statement based on Poblacion (Bolinao town) speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Persons 1978 states his data are 'basically from the Poblacion of Bolinao' (municipal centre), noting minor differences from Santiago Island and Anda speech; same language as Glottolog boli1256 (no sub-dialect codes in Glottolog).

sources.note: Sec. 1.4 'Stress group': stress = increased intensity + slight pitch rise + length on open syllables; 'The occurrence of stress in any word is unpredictable but.. one of the three last syllables of the stress group'; under affixation stress keeps its position relative to the last syllable; length is the minimal difference between many words (sa.lay 'egg' vs salay 'tree'); secondary stress predictable from primary; orthography omits suprasegmentals.
